Held to the records by scripts/release-report/limitations.test.mjs: 'reviewed' is the sha256 of the record as it was read, so any edit to a record -- a status line naming a later record included -- fails until it is read again and stamped with 'node scripts/release-report/limitations.mjs --stamp NNNN'. A line can outlive its truth until its record changes; 'heldBy' names a test that shows it still holds, and the release report fails a run in which that test did not pass. The wording is held by review.

limitations.says: The `@formancy` scope mixes formancy's Apache-2.0 packages with this module's source-available ones, so a dependency audit reads each package's licence rather than its scope.
The published packages depend on upstream `@formancy/*` at exact versions, so an upstream fix reaches an installation only through a release of this module that moves the version.

0003.none: Its user-facing cost, that what is tested is the images of each engine's matrix and no other, is the report's tested-on section, derived from each run, and 0067's, 0073's and 0074's limitations.

limitations.says: A coverage gap is an aspect of an object with a sentence, so a consumer that wants to act on one has to read the sentence.

0005.none: Its costs -- every change to the business model made in three places, two of them in different SQL dialects, and a minute to start both servers -- fall on contributors.

limitations.says: A PostgreSQL snapshot describes the database as one account sees it, so discovery runs as the account the forms will run as, and snapshots taken by two accounts differ as an access change, not as drift.
PostgreSQL 18 runs the whole adapter suite, but no test is about a `NOT NULL` made `NO INHERIT` or its virtual generated columns.
PostgreSQL defaults and check expressions are kept as the server deparses them, inside the fingerprint, so a major upgrade that deparses one differently reads as drift.
The deparsing functions read the catalog caches, not the discovery transaction's snapshot, so the one-moment guarantee covers the rows and not the spellings of defaults and checks.
PostgreSQL's `enforced` is read from triggers as they fire in an ordinary session; a session with `session_replication_role = replica` skips them, and nothing in the snapshot can say so.
A form told a SQL Server `datetime` has three digits accepts `.001`, which the server stores as `.000`, and one told `smalldatetime` keeps seconds sees them rounded to the minute, silently.
SQL Server's `money` is described as a `decimal(19,4)` whose upper part it cannot hold, and the server refuses such a value.
SQL Server discovery is several queries side by side, not one consistent read, so a concurrent `ALTER` can tear it.
SQL Server discovery's queries name catalog views and columns a release outside the matrix may not have.
A client sends exact decimals as strings, which an ordinary JSON client does not do by default.
A value is canonicalised to its column's scale, so the API changes what it was sent: `12.5` comes back `12.50`.
Decimal fields are text inputs, with no numeric keyboard hint and no spinner, and totals over money are not offered, because formancy has no decimal-safe expression.
A form for a table with a version-looking column is create-only until somebody confirms the column.
Generated labels are de-snaked column names, a starting point and nothing more.
Any change to a lookup's foreign key stops the lookup, including `ON DELETE`, which only a delete of the lookup's target exercises.
A new gap on the root's columns stops writes even when every bound column is still visible.
A server upgrade that respells a type stops every form that binds it.
Writability is per operation, so a tightened field stops all of update, even a patch that does not touch it.
Drift leaves out changes outside the form, so an empty report beside two different fingerprints is normal, and no schema-wide diff exists.
Rename hints compare definitions only: two same-typed columns renamed at once give crossed hints, and a rename that also changed the type gives none.
Drift review does not compare triggers or check expressions as validation, and between rescans only the runtime's comparison of the form's own table at each request (0041) sees a change.
Drift's sentences are English and not a contract; its `kind` is.

Equality is all a row filter can say, on the form's own row or, through a lookup, on the row it references (0043): an actor in two tenants at once is not expressible, nor is a rule two foreign-key hops away.
A policy names every field, so a field a regeneration adds is invisible until somebody grants it, and a regeneration that renames a field makes the policy invalid until it is edited.
The trusted context is only as trustworthy as the host that builds it: a host that builds it from a request body defeats every check.
A text key of forty non-ASCII characters, or twenty emoji, cannot be offered as a lookup at all; such a row is counted in `omitted` and cannot be chosen.
Lookup membership compares spellings, so a saved answer naming a key the database has since re-cased is refused on the next save.
A foreign key onto a boolean, a time or a timestamp key cannot be offered as a lookup.
A person who sees a date in a lookup label cannot search for it.
Lookup paging is by offset, which costs a scan up to the offset on both engines.
The order of text is each engine's collation, so a lookup lists non-ASCII text in an order that differs by engine.
Lookup labels are not unique: two customers called "Acme AG" look alike, and only the token tells them apart.
Nothing caps the lookup page size an administrator configures.
The file configuration store serves one instance: over NFS, two instances on a shared volume could both believe they lost a compare-and-swap.
Finding a form's newest version reads its directory, which is linear in the number of versions.
Rotating a key named by `FORMANCY_DATA_IDENTITY_SECRET` or `FORMANCY_DATA_IDENTITY_PUBLIC_KEY_FILE` is a restart; only a key set file is read again without one (0059).

A host with no backend of its own cannot sign a token: it calls the data server with tokens its identity provider issues, carrying the claims the operator maps, from an origin the operator lists (0060).
Roles and attributes are only as fine-grained as the host's token; the server cannot ask anybody anything else.
Every record read converts every column to text in SQL, which is slower than letting the driver parse.
A failed update costs a second query to tell `stale` from `not-found`.

On PostgreSQL, a filter on a column whose type's `=` is not pg_catalog's, such as `citext`, compares case-sensitively and matches fewer rows than its own `=` would, and one with no cast to text, such as `hstore`, is refused.

A PostgreSQL value no shape of formancy's names -- `infinity`, a BC or five-digit year, a time of `24:00`, a NaN -- reaches the form as text the codec refuses, so a date or a number of this kind sent back on save is refused until the person changes it.
PostgreSQL search folds case but not accents, and folds through the database's default collation rather than the column's own.
PostgreSQL text sorts in the column's collation, which on the tested image is code point order; the same data on a glibc image orders differently.
On PostgreSQL, `unknown-outcome` is also reported for a cut while the server is still parsing, which wrote nothing.
PostgreSQL's 40003 is mapped to `unknown-outcome` and 23001 to `foreign-key-violation` without a test that provokes them.
An update trusts that the identity is a key: an identity that is not unique would change every matching row, and the adapter throws afterwards rather than before.
The PostgreSQL adapter refuses a name longer than 63 bytes, the default build's limit, which a server compiled with a larger `NAMEDATALEN` allows.
Nothing bounds how many tokens a PostgreSQL `resolve` or `rejects` is handed: past 65,533 parameters postgres.js throws, which fails closed but not gracefully.
On SQL Server, `returning` is the row as the statement wrote it, before an AFTER trigger changed it; only the version is read back after one.
A SQL Server record with no identity, or with a key column that is not text, an integer, a decimal, a uuid or a date, keeps the version its statement saw.
A trigger's `RAISERROR` refuses the write on SQL Server even where the customer's own application lets it commit as a warning.
A SQL Server table with an enabled INSTEAD OF trigger for an operation cannot be written that way through this adapter, nor can a table whose account is denied VIEW DEFINITION on it.
A SQL Server view made writable by an INSTEAD OF trigger cannot be written through this adapter either.
A SQL Server trigger that commits or rolls back the transaction and raises nothing makes its write `unknown-outcome`, though a retry would often be safe.
On SQL Server, an AFTER trigger that deletes the row it fired for leaves `ok: true` over a table that does not hold it.
A value read from a widened SQL Server column may be one the snapshot's codec would not accept.
SQL Server names a constraint or a column only in English, and in a translated session a 547 whose constraint name holds the other kind's keyword as a word of its own is misread.
A SQL Server trigger that throws one of the adapter's own error numbers, from 51701, with the adapter's exact message is misread.
A record token tells anyone who may read the record its key, whatever the policy says about the key's field, and a create-only actor gets the key of what it made.
A record whose key no token can carry, such as forty non-ASCII characters, a timestamp or a float, is readable by nobody through this module.
The planner is strict: a JSON boolean for the three-state select, `'true'` for a checkbox, an empty patch, a changed key and a tenant attribute of `'042'` are refused, and `PATCH {}` is an error.
A table whose only version column is part of its key cannot be updated through this module.
`validatePolicy` accepts a row filter on the version column, so that mistake shows at the first save and not at publication.
Every request is checked against its snapshot from scratch, a pass over the bindings per request that has not been measured.
The connection registry holds one pool per connection for the server's lifetime, so a deployment with many rarely used connections pays for idle pools.
A connection cannot be created through the API: adding a database is a change to a reviewed file and a restart.
Administration is as granular as one list of roles and, under review, a second for publishers: everyone who may propose may also see every connection's metadata and, without review, publish.
The administrator plane's 503 tells the caller nothing actionable, so an administrator debugging a connection reads the server log.
An administrator is a user of the host application; formancy's own admin users and sessions are not consulted.

In `@formancy/core`, at 0.3.0 and again at 0.4.0 and 0.5.0, an answer is checked once `validate()` has run and on every change after that, so a person typing into an untouched form sees nothing until they press Validate.
Every update reads the record first, one extra query, and an actor who may update and not read gets no echo removed and must send only writable fields.
A lookup query says which operation the form is open for, which a client has to know.
The audit trail is not evidence: an event is written after the database commits, by a different system, so a crash between the two loses it, and nothing stops a privileged operator editing the log.
Without an audit key, two events about one record cannot be told to be about the same record.
There is no list of published forms: the studio's drift step asks for a form id.
The studio's preview shows no lookup options; the list is the runtime plane's, under the published policy.
Reloading the studio signs the administrator out, and a token that expires mid-work turns every request into the server's 401.
A deployment serves the studio's files and `/v1` from one origin, or the studio cannot sign in.

A deployment that wants its own pool, with custom sizes or a TLS setup the options do not express, goes through the adapters' connect functions, whose options are deliberately few, and cannot pass in a driver built elsewhere.
The browser's `maxLength` is looser than a UTF-8 or code-page `varchar`, which is checked on the server only, and stricter than PostgreSQL for emoji.
A code-page `varchar` is checked only by characters; on a double-byte code page the save decides.
A collation change on a bound `varchar` blocks its form until it is reviewed, though reads would still work.
A by-default identity, a `serial` column and a sequence-default key cannot be set from a form, though the column allows it.
A SQL Server sequence default whose definition the account may not read cannot be told from an ordinary default, and stays writable.
A 32-bit float's answer is not always what was sent: `0.123456789` comes back `0.12345679`.
A move between two code pages that are not UTF-8, such as 1252 to 932, is seen neither by drift nor by the fingerprint.
A SQL Server `datetime` reads rounded to the millisecond, by SQL Server.
SQL Server's `is_not_for_replication` is not read.
Binary columns have no codec.
A SQL Server snapshot carries a row-security gap unless the account holds database VIEW DEFINITION and no VIEW DEFINITION or CONTROL deny on any object or schema.
A snapshot's capabilities are what was true at discovery: a grant revoked later fails at runtime as `permission-denied` until drift review sees it.
That row security `applies` says nothing about which rows, so a changed policy expression is not drift.
A view is not followed to its tables: a read through one may be refused while its columns say SELECT, and the generator offers such a view.
The privilege functions and `row_security_active` read live catalog state, so a GRANT or an ALTER committed mid-discovery can make an answer a moment later than the rows beside it.
A row-security policy that reads the login rather than the user is not followed, and a login change is not in the fingerprint.
REFERENCES and EXECUTE privileges are not described.
A PostgreSQL `serial` or `nextval` default needs USAGE on its sequence, which is not described, so such a create fails `permission-denied`.
A field written on create only is not disabled on update, because formancy has no per-operation mode; the server refuses a changed value.
Drift compares the scope's schemas case-sensitively, so on a case-insensitive SQL Server database whose scope is configured as `SALES` a missing root reads as `scope-narrowed`.
On SQL Server, a `char` or `varchar` filter under a `SQL_` collation scans rather than seeks.
Labels are not localised: a person reads `true`, an instant in UTC to the second and a time to the minute, cut and never rounded.
Boolean row filters are refused, in lookups too: a policy that filtered by a flag must use a column a filter can compare.
A policy whose lookup filters by a boolean column is refused at publish.
A policy whose root row filter names a boolean column is refused at publish too.
`refused` lumps a broken trigger with a business rule; the person reads one sentence, and the message is for the log.
Most transient error codes are allowlisted by documentation and not provoked by any test.
Drift blocks a lookup on a widening of a column it reads by too, until the form is published again.
A SQL Server `varchar` created under `ANSI_PADDING OFF` refuses a trailing space as `out-of-range`.
Search folding differs by engine: a filter matches the same rows on both, a search does not.
Every name a published form carries gets a server-backed option source, and a name the server does not know fails closed.
Records are addressed by token only: the definition does not say which columns identify a record.
The server's sentences are English; a host that shows another language maps the codes itself.
On the host page, "Load the saved record" discards the draft, and nothing merges.
A press during a save sends nothing and is not queued, and the form is not locked during a save.
A column rename loses its presentation overrides: the old label is reported `field-gone`, and a person carries it across by hand.
A generator release that renames a section reports that section's overrides as `section-gone`.
A root whose own label is `Record` loses its section overrides when its main or system section comes or goes.
A pin taken out of a stored request by hand is not caught on read.
Regenerated forms place new fields by the generator's neighbour, not where a person would put them, and keep a person's label where both changed, which can keep a stale one.
A dropped field's place in an order is not reported.
A server upgraded between propose and publish refuses the draft, which is proposed again.
Anything outside the presentation edits is refused at publish: help text, translations, new sections and a numeric span.
A restore brings back that version's policy; it is not a database rollback.
The runtime stops what drift blocks in the form's own table only; what drift blocks for a lookup's table, privileges, row security or the account is stopped at review alone (0041).
A publish conflict is a rebase onto the other version, not a merge.
Publish does not build each lookup's configuration, so a lookup that cannot be configured fails at runtime.

"It may have been saved" is also said where nothing was: a cut while PostgreSQL parses or a SQL Server write waits, a KILL, a trigger that rolls back and raises, a data server that is down, or a proxy's page on a save.

The write id holds in one process: a resend that reaches another replica, arrives after a restart or after its answer left the bounded store, or comes from a client that sends no id, is applied again.
Kept answers hold the record's values in memory for ten minutes.
A create whose key the database numbers cannot be reconciled, so a person who confirms "Enter it again anyway" may make a duplicate.
`unchanged` means not visible yet: on PostgreSQL an orphaned write can still commit after the check.
`absent` is what the read shows through the person's read filter, so a stored row the filter hides, or whose key a trigger rewrote, is `absent` too.
`present` is a row with that key, which another person's create of the same key also is.
`reconcile` needs read permission: a person who may create and not read gets the read's refusal.
A write whose answer the page lost in transport is audited as `ok`.
The hold on an unknown create belongs to the form: New or Load clears it, and nothing stops the person entering the same record into the new form.
A 4xx with a sentence and no code is taken as a refusal, so a proxy that answered a write with such a JSON body would be believed.
A server shutting down after a cut waits up to five seconds on PostgreSQL for a statement that will never answer.

The composed stack is not a production deployment: no TLS, loopback only, HS256 with a minted token, one replica, a file store on a local volume, SQL Server's Developer edition, fixture data, secrets as plain files and nothing restarted after a reboot.
The composed stack's `down -v` destroys the secrets too, and with them every token signed by the old key.
The composed stack needs Compose 2.20 or later.
Docker Desktop, Windows and macOS are run by no gate, and neither are the seeds' bind mounts there.
Nothing clicks through the composed stack in a browser: the guide's clicks are held by the apps' suites against the real server in jsdom.
The server's 500 for a configuration store it cannot write names the path.
The administrator plane's audit sink is required, while the runtime plane's stays optional.

An administrator request whose connection is not allowlisted, or whose form id does not have the shape, is audited with that part `null`, and so is every read of a stored version whose connection left the allowlist.
A request whose client left is audited with the status the server answered.
A body Fastify refuses is audited naming no actor, an administrator's included.
The request log no longer says which path a request addressed.
An administrator-plane event is written after the store's swap commits, so a crash in between loses it, and a sink that fails is logged while the publish stands.
A route that never finishes writes no audit event, and neither does a process killed while a route runs.
That every audited request writes exactly one event rests on what was measured on Fastify 5.12.5 and Node 22; a Fastify or Node that changed either behaviour would lose an event.
A request that never reaches a route of either plane is not audited: a 404 or a 414 from the router, a URL that does not decode, the 503 while the server closes, and what Node's parser refuses.
The audit trail does not say what changed between two versions, and does not record the bundle, the policy or a snapshot.
`/health`, `/v1/whoami` and CORS preflights are not audited.
Every request of the administrator plane is a log line, the studio's page loads and every refused probe included, a volume not measured.

On PostgreSQL every lookup search reads every row its form's row filter admits -- each of the tenant's customers, or the whole referenced table on a form with no tenant row filter -- because no index serves a contains search or the order by name.
On SQL Server every lookup search reads every row its form's row filter admits too, by seeks over the tenant's keys, or by a scan of the whole referenced table on a form with no tenant row filter.
No trigram index, prefix mode or minimum search length ships, so every lookup search reads every row its filter admits; the lookup deadline caps how long it runs, not how much it reads (0061).

Every adapter statement makes two database round trips, because mssql checks each pooled connection with `SELECT 1` before using it and postgres.js has the server describe each unprepared statement before running it.

`FORMANCY_DATA_RATE_LIMIT` sets the requests a minute per client address, and behind a proxy `FORMANCY_DATA_TRUSTED_PROXIES` does not name it raises the one bucket every client behind that proxy shares (0071).

The published performance figures describe one machine as its hypervisor presents it: loopback HTTP, the databases through Docker's published ports, no TLS, warm caches, both images' default settings, SQL Server's Developer edition, PostgreSQL on musl, one server process, the order form on the writer's account and one page size.

Not measured: tails under an arrival rate, more requests in flight than the pools hold, a lookup table between or beyond the two sizes measured, a customer table not loaded in key order, a larger snapshot, the Alpine image, the composed stack's proxy, and PostgreSQL under a default isolation other than READ COMMITTED, where every record request locks the form's table first (0041).

The time of the description of the form's table that every record request reads (0041) is inside the published figures and not separated from them; a write refused as drift is counted and never timed.

Contention from outside the measuring VM is not seen, and contention during a block's own load cannot be told from that load, because the hypervisor reports no steal and the calibration probe is read only in the idle gaps around each block.
The database's CPU per request is net of its container's idle rate in the gaps around the block, so work the engine did on its own only while the block ran is still in it.
The added-latency figures cover the leg between the server and the database; the browser's leg to the server, TLS, bandwidth and TCP's congestion window are not in them.

An added-latency difference includes what the machine drifted between a request's undelayed and delayed passes, which run one after the other: for some requests it moved between rounds by more than a tenth of the added delay, and more samples did not remove that.

Nothing in the product refuses a server version that discovery can read and no test ran: what a release says it was tested on is not what it accepts; the connection test, the studio and drift review say so.
The images are moving tags, so two runs of one commit can test, and report, different server builds.
That a test declaring a shared case asserts that case is held by review; the report counts the declaration.
A limitation in this register can outlive its truth until a later record changes the record that states it: the register is held to the records by hash, not to the code.
A release's SBOM names what cdxgen finds, which on 2026-10-09 left out tedious, the package under mssql that speaks TDS to SQL Server.

0036.none: A rule for this repository's branches; nobody who installs, integrates or operates the module meets it.

limitations.says: Behind Cloudflare, Cloudflare decrypts every request and answer at its edge, host tokens and record values included, and anybody with Cloudflare Tunnel edit permission or an unrevoked login token can stream every request header, so that permission is as sensitive as reading host tokens.

The tunnel is locally managed, against Cloudflare's recommendation for most uses and for Docker, so its routes cannot be edited in the dashboard, and each setup run makes an account-wide login token the operator must revoke by hand, which cloudflared leaves to the browser to download when it cannot fetch it.

Whoever can change the tunnel's ingress, or add a private network route to it, which no setting of cloudflared refuses, reaches the web front's both ports without Access and whatever the machine routes to, though not the server past nginx or the composed stack's databases; setup looks for a private network route once, and nothing looks again.

The data server answers 400 `path-not-plain`, before authentication, to a path holding a percent-escape, a backslash, an empty segment or a `.` or `..` segment, where a route used to answer 401, 404 or 400.

What Fastify's router answers before any hook -- an escape that does not decode, a parameter past its length, the 503 while closing -- carries no `Cache-Control: no-store` and is not counted by the rate limit.

Behind Cloudflare, an edge error, a block, a challenge or a lapsed Access session reads in data-client as a write that may have been saved and a read it does not understand, though nothing reached the server and nothing is audited.

On Cloudflare's Free plan the edge's rate-limiting rule cannot answer with a body of its own, so a write it blocked reads as one that may have been saved; the body that reads as a refusal needs Pro or above.

Behind the tunnel the server counts each visitor by the address Cloudflare's edge reported, because the composed stack names cloudflared and nginx as proxies (0071); the edge's rule counts per Cloudflare location and imprecisely, and both count a host application's backend as one visitor.
nginx's access log holds every visitor's address as Cloudflare forwards it, and every request line with its query.

Nothing of the Cloudflare deployment has been measured through a real tunnel: what Access answers, whether the edge forwards an encoded path as sent, whether log streaming shows `Authorization`, and how long the tunnel takes to connect are documented or unknown.

0038.none: Its costs are the repository's and CI's: the pictures' bytes, retaking them when a pictured sentence changes, and the pictures job's time. Nobody who installs, integrates or operates the module meets them.

limitations.says: A client that publishes a regeneration sends back in `keysConfirmed` each reassigned key whose grants it keeps, or the server refuses the version, so a client that ignored `keysReassigned` is refused whenever its policy gives a role on such a key.

The check compares a publish with the version it replaces and no other: grants removed in one version and given back in the next are not asked about, so one policy file pushed twice, the first time without the reassigned keys, carries the first version's grants to the columns those keys name now.

Keys are compared by the name of the column or foreign key they stand for, not its table: a publish that moves a form to another root table or connection carries every grant to the same-named column there, unasked. The studio starts such a draft from an empty policy.
Which reassigned keys an administrator confirmed is kept in neither the version file nor the audit trail, and under review only in the draft it was submitted with.
A publish over a version the server no longer serves, because its file does not parse or does not validate, a stricter validator after an upgrade included, is not checked for reassigned keys.
Versions published before this check are not checked again, and a restore of one brings back whatever grants its publish let through.

The studio offers Keep and Remove only for the keys its regeneration reported, so a draft proposed afresh, or generated again after a key renumbered once more, whose policy gives a role on such a key is refused with the server's sentences, a Keep left from the regeneration confirming the column it reported and not the one the key names now; it is published by removing those grants or by regenerating from the Drift step.
A form shows an instant to the second and a time to the minute on both engines, PostgreSQL now as SQL Server already did, so a stored fraction and seconds stay in the database and are not shown.
An instant or a time that differs from the stored value only below the second or the minute cannot be written through a form: it is taken for an unedited echo and removed from the update.
An actor who may write an instant or a time and not read it, or who may update a record and not read it, has nothing removed, so a cut value they send back replaces the stored fraction or seconds.
An instant the person changes is written in UTC, so SQL Server stores it at +00:00 whatever offset the row held.

An instant of `infinity` or a time of `24:00`, which PostgreSQL holds and no shape names, cannot be submitted through either renderer until the person changes it; a client of its own that sends it back unedited saves, and the value is kept.
A form whose only writable fields are instants and times, saved unedited, is refused as `nothing-to-update` and writes nothing, which the host page shows under "Not saved".

An update carrying an instant or a time the actor may write and read is refused with the read's own answer when the read before it failed, whatever the failure, though the write itself might have succeeded.

A caller of `planUpdate` that sends an instant or a time the actor may read must pass the record as read, or the update is refused `record-not-read`; an update request built for an adapter without the planner is held to no echo rule.

A write that arrives again with its write id is answered with a refusal of its own, not the first sending's answer, when the form cannot be loaded or the connection opened, and on create when a lookup cannot vouch for a selection: those answers come before the sending.
An instant changed in `@formancy/react`'s datetime control is saved as the local minute the control holds, its seconds and fraction gone; Angular's control was not measured.

The runtime compares only a form's own table -- its kind, columns, keys and foreign keys -- with the database at each request; what drift review blocks for a lookup's table, a privilege, row security or the account is stopped at review alone, the database still enforcing privileges and row security itself, and the studio says which blocked operations the server still allows.
Drift refuses per operation at runtime as in review: a tightened field stops every update of the form, including one that does not touch it, until the form is republished.
Lookups are searched and resolved whatever drift says of the form's table.

A column dropped and added again under the same name and definition, a version column included, or the table dropped and created again so, is seen neither by drift review nor by the runtime; a write in flight across it is refused, and the next is not.
Drift review calls a form unreadable when its confirmed concurrency token is out of sight behind a gap, as it does when the token is dropped.

Opening a form, creating, and updating as someone who may not read the record each make one more database statement than before, to read the table's definition, and every write checks the definition again inside its statement.

Every describe, read and write reads the form's table's catalog inside its statement: measured on 2026-10-10 on one shared machine, on PostgreSQL 4.3 to 6.2 ms of the server's time for a describe or a read where a read took 0.14 to 0.17 ms, and 3.3 to 5 ms for a write where it took 0.14 to 0.25 ms; on SQL Server 1.4 to 2.6 ms of CPU where a read took 0.1 ms and a write 0.66 to 0.77 ms. Nothing pins the figures until 0034's harness measures them.
A change to the form's table that lands between that description and the write refuses the request with `schema-changed`, even when drift review would call it harmless; sending it again is answered.
Opening a form asks the database, so a form whose database cannot be reached is refused with 503 instead of opened.

On PostgreSQL under a default isolation other than READ COMMITTED, every read and write takes the table's lock first in a transaction of its own, and an account granted columns of the table and nothing on the table cannot take that lock and is refused `permission-denied`.

On PostgreSQL under a default isolation other than READ COMMITTED a request makes more round trips than under READ COMMITTED -- counted through the server on 2026-10-10, a read 7 where it is 2, a create 9 where it is 6, and an update by someone who may read 12 where it is 4 -- and nothing pins the figures.
On PostgreSQL a pooled connection whose isolation differs from the one a request was described on refuses its write as `unavailable`, and nothing is written.

On PostgreSQL, in a pool whose connections differ in isolation, a write that wrote nothing can be answered with another cause than the one that refused it, because the statement that tells them apart runs on any connection; nothing is written either way.

On PostgreSQL the runtime spells a column's type as discovery does, under its connection's `search_path`; a pool whose connections differ in it can see a changed type drift review did not, and refuses that form's requests with `drift`.
On PostgreSQL a refused write still fires the table's statement-level triggers, and what they did is kept; SQL Server rolls it back.

On SQL Server an account the catalog hides the form's table from, denied VIEW DEFINITION, cannot have the table described, so every request of a form running as it is refused `schema-changed`, reads included.
On SQL Server a connection whose TEXTSIZE is shorter than a table's description cannot describe it, and every request of the form is refused `unavailable`.

On SQL Server a column given dynamic data masking after the form was published is read as its mask by an account without UNMASK, and neither drift review nor the runtime compares masking, so a save that sends every field writes the mask over the stored value.
A whole-number field accepts a fraction in the browser and only the server's codec refuses it, because generated forms stay on spec 3, which has no `step`.

A TypeScript host whose renderer is at `@formancy/*` 0.3.0 casts `@formancy/data-client`'s published form to its own `FormSchema` or moves to 0.4.0 or later, because the client's types are `@formancy/spec` 0.5.0's, whose `specVersion` admits `"4"`.

That a host whose reader is at `@formancy/*` 0.3.0 reads the generated forms was measured by hand, in scratch checks over the forms each generated from the committed snapshots, on 2026-10-10 and again on 2026-10-16 once generated lookups carried a typeahead (0066); other forms were not generated, and nothing here runs a 0.3.0 renderer.
A child form's tenant rule restates its parent's in its lookup filter, and nothing checks that the two agree.
A form is reached through one foreign-key hop at most: a grandchild is not scoped by its grandparent.
A row whose through key is NULL is reachable by nobody, so a through field is required on create, omitted or null, whatever its column allows.
For the same reason a through field may not be cleared on update, whatever its column allows.
A through over a lookup that offers every row, or over a text key, is refused at publish on both engines, the text key until a snapshot records collations.
What a child's create pins is a parent the person may reference, not the one on their screen.
A server older than this release refuses a policy that uses `through`, as it refuses every property it does not read.
Each through adds an EXISTS to every read, update and not-found statement of its form, whose plan and time are not measured.

On PostgreSQL, under READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ, an update that waits for its row while another transaction moves the row's parent out of the scope and commits is written, where a row filter on the row itself and SQL Server answer not-found.
A key a through names is a grant for 0039's check, so a publish that re-points it to another foreign key is refused until confirmed even when nobody holds a role on its field.

By how both engines run an offset and a sort, and not measured here, a list page reads every row before its offset, and a page sorted by a column no index serves reads every row its filters admit -- the whole table on a form with no tenant row filter.
A list has no total, and a row inserted or removed before the offset between two pages shows one row twice or skips one.
A list is sorted and searched by the form's own column fields only, never by a lookup's label.
A list's text is ordered by each engine's collation, so a page of non-ASCII names can come in a different order on each engine.
A form whose key can be NULL, or whose key is held in a field the person may not read, offers that person no list, only a record by its token.

A form whose policy has no row filter and no through while a lookup's options are filtered offers no list -- every child form published before through existed, until it is republished with one, and a policy that means its rows are shared, which has no way to say so.
A row whose key does not fit a token is listed in its place and cannot be opened.

Nothing bounds a list's statement: on SQL Server the driver's default request timeout, which this module does not set, is expected to end a long one as `unavailable` as it ends a read -- inferred for a list, not tested -- on PostgreSQL it runs to its end, and on both the database finishes a list the browser abandoned.

A list sorted by a column outside the key that was made nullable since its snapshot places its NULLs as each engine does until drift is reviewed: last ascending on PostgreSQL, first ascending on SQL Server.

A key column made nullable, or a key dropped, since a form was published refuses every page of its records as drift until the form is reviewed, though drift review reports a nullable key column only as a note.

A list narrowed to a parent over a text foreign key matches as the database's equality does: case-insensitively under a case-insensitive collation on SQL Server, exactly under PostgreSQL's default collation.
No list is in the published performance figures: what a page reads, its round trips and its time are not measured.

Each request for the menu of forms reads and validates every published form, with nothing cached: about 2 ms a form, 180 ms over a hundred forms of the fixture snapshot's size, measured once in-process on 2026-10-11, those the person may not read included. Any host token can ask for it, and nothing bounds that work but the server's one rate limit.
One form directory the file store cannot read fails its listing, and the menu of forms is then a 500 for everybody; read from the store's code, not tested.

A published version that no longer validates, does not parse or cannot be read, or is bound to a connection the allowlist does not have, is left out of the menu of forms, and only the server's log says so.
A form a person may create with and not read is not in their menu of forms.

The menu of forms says what the policy and the published bundles allow, not what the database allows now: a form it names can be refused as drift when opened, and a child it names can be offered no list then.
A foreign key onto a key other than the parent form's identity, or of another type than the key it references, makes no child in the menu of forms, though its rows reference the parent's.
Under a collation that ignores case or trailing spaces, a child form's rows listed under a parent record can spell a text foreign key otherwise than the parent's token does.
The studio's and the host page's third-party notices are the texts each bundled package ships; what a licence requires beyond its text is not judged.
The helpers Vite and Rolldown write into the studio's and the host page's chunks themselves are not listed in their third-party notices.

What Vite folds into the studio's or the host page's output as text is not listed in its third-party notices: a package stylesheet that a stylesheet `@import`s, a package's file under Vite's inline limit named by a CSS `url()` or a `new URL()`, and a module whose only export is a boolean or a number.
Code a package vendors is listed in the third-party notices under the package that ships it, with the licence and notice files on the way to it, not under its own name and version.
The web front serves each page's third-party notices but not the repository's own LICENSE.md and NOTICE, which are in the web image at /usr/share/formancy-data/.
The third-party notices at /studio/THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt and /host/THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt name the exact version of every package each page bundles, to anyone who reaches the web front.
The host page's grids are React's, AG Grid Community pinned to one release, and show a page at a time with no total.
A record is never in the host page's address: a reload or a shared link opens the form and its layout, not the record.
On the host page, leaving unsaved work -- another row, New record, Load, another form, Back, Sign out, a child row, hiding a renderer -- asks first; a browser reload or a closed tab does not.
A child row's parent is fixed only on the host page: the server checks only that it is one the person may reference.
A form a person may only read still draws Save on the host page: its fields are disabled, and the server refuses the update.
AG Grid's focused cell is a one-pixel border that forced colours do not draw, and a focused cell's change of state is not announced.
The host page's workspace, AG Grid in it, is a chunk of about a megabyte minified and 300 kB gzipped, loaded after sign-in: measured once, on 2026-10-11.
The renderer choice and the split are kept in each viewer's browser, so a shared machine keeps the last viewer's.

The host page's grid columns are sized to their content -- the first page's, and the rows shown each time the split is let go -- and never stretched to the lane's width, so a wider lane leaves its space at the end.

The host gate decides what axe cannot inside a grid on the pixels each browser painted, and accepts columns past the window's edge inside a grid's own scroller while the grid's well stays inside the window.
The composed stack's order form account may not read sales.order_line, so the getting-started guide and the README's pictures show no child grid.

The licence in force has not been reviewed by a lawyer: where the free rights end and Production Use begins, what Redistribution covers, and termination rest on terms no lawyer has read, and a production licence is a separate written agreement whose terms are not published.
Production licences are requested at the address section 9 of LICENSE.md names, and no price is published.

Open, and a lawyer's questions: which court the Rightsholder's domicile in Switzerland names, and whether it is exclusive; whether Version 1 replaces Version 0 for someone who received the Software under Version 0, and what a later version does for someone who received it under Version 1; whether the licence's law and court govern a production licence; and whether the UN Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods applies.
A snapshot taken before 0049 says neither whether its account may delete from a table nor what refers to it; only a new discovery records them.

A SQL Server account without database VIEW DEFINITION, or with a VIEW DEFINITION or CONTROL deny on any object or schema, cannot establish that it sees every foreign key that refers to a table in scope, and its snapshot carries a `referenced-by` gap.
A table outside the approved schemas whose foreign key refers to one in scope is named in the snapshot, with its key and columns.
A PostgreSQL key onto a partition of a table, or onto a table that inherits from it, is not listed on that table but said by a `referenced-by` gap on it, for every account.
A SQL Server graph edge constraint is not listed as something that refers to a node table; each one that connects it is a `referenced-by` gap on it, for every account.
A server older than 0049 refuses a snapshot with a `referenced-by` gap, and so a form published from one, on every read.
A record is deleted one at a time, by its token and the version it was read at; a form without a confirmed concurrency token offers no delete.
A table whose version column the module maintains offers no delete unless the database numbers a column of its key, so the fixture's order lines, whose key people type, offer none on PostgreSQL.
A form offers delete only once it is regenerated and republished from a snapshot this release took.
A role that may delete must be granted read with the same form.

A policy may grant delete over another table's foreign key that cascades onto the form's table, clears its references or sets them to a default only where its `cascades` names that key with its action (0051): without it, the fixture's orders, whose lines and deliveries cascade, and its deliveries, whose parcels do, cannot be deleted.
A delete cannot be undone here, and the audit trail keeps only a keyed hash of its token, or nothing without an audit key.
A delete refused because other rows refer to the record says so, and names none of them.
Triggers that run on a delete are not seen, shown or governed: only an INSTEAD OF trigger on SQL Server and a delete PostgreSQL declined are refused.
A row an AFTER DELETE trigger inserts again is reported deleted.

On PostgreSQL a rule that acts on a delete makes every delete of its table refused, a soft delete written as a rule included: PostgreSQL refuses the delete's statement under most rules, and the statement's own guard under an unconditional DO INSTEAD rule that returns a row.
On PostgreSQL a delete that waits for its row while another transaction moves the row's parent out of the person's scope deletes it; SQL Server answers not found.

On PostgreSQL a version column moves only through this module's writes, so another application's delete and insert again of a typed key restarts it, and an update with the old version lands on the new record.
On PostgreSQL every delete reads pg_constraint, which has no index for the lookup, so its cost grows with the constraints of the whole database; not measured past the fixture's.

A server older than 0050 refuses a policy that grants delete, and this release's client answers `unexpected` to a form reply from a server older than 0050, which carries no `deleting`, so a host upgrades its server first.

A delete that cascades into other tables, or clears their references, is offered only where the policy's `cascades` names each such foreign key with its action and the account may DELETE from every table it reaches; the rows it reaches are asked of no form's policy.
A cascade or a SET NULL into a table outside the approved schemas, and a SET NULL whose cleared column another key follows by an ON UPDATE that acts, are refused even where the policy names the key.
On both engines a cascade deletes the rows it reaches whatever the deleting account's row security says of them, FORCE included on PostgreSQL, a filter or a block predicate on SQL Server.

A delete is held to the account's DELETE on every table it reaches, though neither engine asks it for a cascade and PostgreSQL's lock is taken with any grant to write: an account that lost DELETE there is refused, whatever other grant it kept, and nothing is deleted.
A reference a delete clears does not move the referring row's version column, so a person editing that row is not told it changed; a rowversion moves.

A new foreign key that acts on a delete of any table a delete reaches, an accepted key whose action changed, and DELETE revoked on any of those tables refuse every delete of the form until it is reviewed and republished.

On PostgreSQL a delete that reaches past its record locks every table it reaches, ROW EXCLUSIVE, before its statement, whatever the isolation, in a transaction of its own; how many round trips that costs is not measured.

A delete that reaches past its record and whose answer is lost is unknown, and what it left depends on where the answer was lost: on PostgreSQL, lost before the commit was sent, nothing of it was committed; on SQL Server, lost after the batch committed, all of it. A PostgreSQL answer lost after the commit was sent, and a SQL Server one lost before the commit, are not tested.

On PostgreSQL a cascaded table's BEFORE DELETE triggers and its rules run as that table's owner, with the owner's grants, and may do what the deleting account could not; its AFTER DELETE triggers run as the deleting account on 15 to 17 and as the owner on 18. Neither is seen nor refused here.
On SQL Server a cascaded table's triggers run as the deleting account, and are neither seen nor refused here.
No delete is measured: the performance page has no figure for one.
A server older than 0051 refuses a policy that names `cascades`.

The studio's list of what a delete also does is as complete as its snapshot says it is, and covers foreign keys only: a trigger or a rule that runs on a delete is not listed, and does what the database defines.

The Policy step lists the keys of the snapshot the form was generated from: a key added since is asked about only once the form is generated again, though drift review reports it, and one that acts blocks delete there.

Where only review sees what blocks a delete -- a key nobody accepted, DELETE revoked on a table it reaches, a gap over what refers to one -- the server still lets a host send deletes until the form is published again: the Drift step says so, with what each delete's own statement still refuses, and not which of those changes it would refuse.
Clearing the roles that may delete leaves the keys accepted, and the policy is refused until each is unticked.
The host page deletes one record at a time, from its open detail or its grid row, after a confirmation in place; no key deletes, and there is no bulk delete and no undo.

The host page's confirmation says whether a delete also deletes or clears other records, and that the database may keep a record others refer to, from what the server says, never which records or how many.
A record a delete cannot find is closed on the host page, never called deleted: it cannot be told from one the person may no longer see.
A grid row's delete names the version the row was listed with, so a record changed since its page was listed is refused as stale until the page is listed again or the record is opened.

While a deletion is out, the record's forms on the host page send nothing on Save; a deletion discarded while out is heard of again in its grid only if it was done, and one discarded while unknown is not heard of again.
In Separate views, a deletion's answer that asks something of the person shows the view it is drawn in, though they had gone to the other.
Every grid of a form that offers delete has one more column, its rows' Delete, which a narrow window reaches only by scrolling the grid.
A row's Delete is dressed by its own style attribute in the room's variables, which the palette guard does not read.
The host's browser gate draws no child row's delete confirmation: on PostgreSQL no child of the fixture's order offers delete, and jsdom holds it on SQL Server alone.
The getting-started guide's form grants no delete, since the studio writes no delete roles yet, so the guide does not delete on the host page.

The separate commercial agreement Redistribution requires is requested at the same address as a production licence, the one section 9 of LICENSE.md names, and its terms and its price are not published.

An image of the composed stack built from a checkout within a day of an upstream release this repository adopted installs that release's `@formancy/*` packages without pnpm's one-day minimum release age, because the build reads this repository's `pnpm-workspace.yaml` and the exemptions in it.

A list ordered by a uuid key, and a lookup's options tied on their label, come in each engine's own order of uuid -- PostgreSQL's by its bytes in turn, SQL Server's by its byte groups, the last six bytes first -- so the same rows are listed in another order on each engine; each order is total and stable.

A grid of records keyed by a uuid, in its default order, lists them in an order that tells a person nothing -- `gen_random_uuid()`'s keys are random, and `newsequentialid()`'s rise only among the keys one server made -- unless the host sorts by another column.

On SQL Server a `newsequentialid()` key rises across every tenant of the server, so a record token tells a tenant that keys were handed out between its own creates, where a `gen_random_uuid()` key on PostgreSQL says nothing of the kind.

A key column with a default that is all of the key the policy does not pin, such as a uuid from `gen_random_uuid()` or `newsequentialid()` alone or beside a pinned tenant, is shown and never written by a generated form, so a person cannot choose it, and a policy that grants write on its field is refused at publish.
A key the database fills beside a column the person gives, such as `(order_id, id)` with nothing pinned, is still written by a generated form, so there the person may choose the uuid.
A one-column key whose default is a constant fills one record, and every later create of that form is refused on the key; inferred from the rule, not tested.

A version column proves a record over a uuid key only where the key is one column filled by gen_random_uuid() on PostgreSQL or newsequentialid() on SQL Server, as the catalog spells it, and no foreign key includes it; a key filled by a constant, uuid_generate_v4(), newid() or any other default, by one of those two beside another key column, or by one of those two on a key that is also a foreign key, offers no delete over a version column.

That gen_random_uuid() and newsequentialid() never hand out one value twice is their design, not something this release measured; a repeat after a delete would start the new record's version where the deleted one's did.

On PostgreSQL a request's description is read under the connection's search_path, so where that path names pg_catalog after a schema holding a function called gen_random_uuid, every delete over a key PostgreSQL's own gen_random_uuid() fills is refused as drift, which drift review does not report.

A row filter on a key column that is the whole key writes the key from the context on every create, so a record deleted is created again under its key by the next create in that context, its version starting where the deleted one's did, as over a by-default identity; inferred from the planner, not tested.

The browser gates run Playwright's builds of Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, headless on Linux: not Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari as people install them, and no browser on macOS, Windows, iOS or Android.

WebKit in the gates is the WPE port with the runner's libsoup networking, not Safari: it moves Tab to links, which Safari does by default only with Option-Tab, and how Safari's network stack treats a lost save is not measured.
Playwright's WebKit names itself Safari on a Mac, so the host page's grids take AG Grid's Safari code paths in the WebKit gate: it proves neither Safari nor a WebKit that is not Safari.

Whether a browser sends a lost save again on its own differs by browser and connection: over HTTP/1.1, when a connection the browser reused closes after the server read the save and before any byte of an answer, Chromium and Firefox send it again and one server process answers that second sending with the first one's answer; WebKit on Linux sends every save on a new connection and never twice, so its page says the save may have been saved.
In Firefox, a click on the host page's or the studio's corner and then Tab goes past the off-screen skip link, because Firefox starts the keyboard from the caret the click left.
No scrollbar took width in the gates' browsers -- Chromium's because Playwright hides them -- so the narrowest widths say nothing of a desktop browser whose scrollbar takes part of the window.

WebKit's networking, TLS and EGL and every leg's fallback fonts come from the runner's image, not from Playwright, so an image update can change what the gates measure; the release report names the versions each run had.
The README's pictures and their text check are Chromium's alone.
On macOS and Windows the gates refuse WebKit, and a machine runs Chromium alone unless FORMANCY_BROWSERS names more; only CI runs every browser, and the report requires each.

In Playwright's WebKit, a pointer press on the host page's Save sent nothing in five of about 175 presses, the document scrolling by 24 px between the press and the release, and the page said nothing of it; the cause was not established, and since then no gate presses Save with a pointer in any browser, so what a person's click on Save meets in a real browser is not checked.

The host gate reads a grid cell's background only where the window shows the cell, scrolling the window to one outside it, which moves what is under the pointer, so a cell can be read under another hover than its state had; a text its grid has scrolled wholly out of view, or covers, is named in the gate's output and not decided.

In WebKit, AG Grid can leave the host page's grid scrolled to the side when the keys that scroll it come faster than WebKit's rendering updates, as a test's do and a person's do not; the host gate waits for a rendering update between such keys, so that case is measured by no gate.

A key set is read again only when the server is sent SIGHUP, and nothing fetches a provider's keys, so a provider's new key verifies only once the operator's file holds it and the server has been signalled.

A key set file that cannot be read, or is refused, when SIGHUP arrives leaves the set in force, a key the file removed included, and only the log says so; the same file stops the next start until it is fixed.
A secret pasted into a key set as `k` as it stands is accepted and verifies no token; `identity-keys-cli.mjs convert` writes the key the server verifies with today.
A key its provider marks for another use or algorithm is left out of force and named in the log, so a signing key the provider re-marks leaves force at the next read.
One algorithm per server: moving a key set to another algorithm, or changing the issuer, the audience or the claim mapping, is a restart.
A token without a `kid` costs one signature check per key in force before it is refused.
An HS256 key's kid that is its own `k`, or 43 base64 characters or more, refuses the key set, because a kid is logged; a 32-byte thumbprint cannot name an HS256 key.

A key set's keys are checked for their length and for the weaknesses under which anyone signs, an RSA exponent of 1 and an Ed25519 point of small order, not for every weak key, and the public key file is not checked for those weaknesses.

A key set file read again that never returns, from a network mount that stalls, holds every SIGHUP after it, which logs nothing until it does, and SIGTERM's exit waits for it; a path that is not a regular file is refused at once.
A server started in a terminal keeps running when the terminal closes, because SIGHUP reads the key set again, or says it read nothing, rather than stopping it.
Where no process can be sent SIGHUP, natively on Windows, a key set is read only at start.
A key set mounted through a Kubernetes `subPath` is never updated, and a secret volume is updated eventually, so a SIGHUP sent before the file changed logs that nothing changed.
A key set file bind-mounted on its own is not seen after it is replaced by a rename; mount its directory.
Each instance of the server reads its key set on its own signal, and only its log says which keys it holds.

A host page on another origin is answered only when its origin is listed exactly; a refused preflight, and a request refused across origins, is a network error to the page, which data-client reads as unreachable or, for a write, unknown though nothing ran, and only the server's log says why.
Across origins a request may carry only Authorization, Content-Type and the write id; a host whose fetch adds another header is refused at the preflight.
No cookie crosses origins, HEAD is not offered, and `/v1/whoami`, `/health` and the administrator's plane answer no other origin.
The reference host page calls only the data server on its own origin.
Chromium may ask the person before a page on a public address calls a server on a private one; this is not tested here.
The origin list is read at start, so adding or removing an origin is a restart.
A browser too old to send `Sec-Fetch-Site` may keep sending requests the server runs to a route for up to the preflight's Max-Age after its origin is removed, without reading the answers.
A deployment that added CORS headers at its own proxy has its cross-origin requests refused until it lists their origins.
Plain-HTTP origins are accepted only on loopback.
Preflights are neither rate-limited by the server nor audited.

A GET, HEAD or POST route of another plane, or an embedder's, whose pattern overlaps any runtime pattern, a route of another method overlapping a runtime pattern of its own method, or any route with a regex parameter, a wildcard or a constraint, stops a server with origins from starting.

No browser gate runs against a server with origins listed: that a browser honours a grant, and is refused after reusing one it cached before its origin was removed, is shown through inject only; the one measurement in browsers, that Chromium and WebKit reuse a URL's grant for another GET, HEAD or POST there, was by hand.

A lookup search still reads every row its filter admits: the lookup deadline caps how long, not how much, so a deployment past the measured size refuses searches with 503 `lookup-timeout` instead of serving them slowly.

The default lookup deadline is the slowest timed lookup answer of one measurement on one machine: SQL Server's tenant search, reading 100,001 rows, eight at a time; a search of a whole table was measured only one at a time, and opening connections and membership checks were not timed, so a slower or larger deployment raises `FORMANCY_DATA_LOOKUP_DEADLINE_MS`.

The lookup deadline starts when the adapter is asked for the statement: reading the form and opening its connection are not bounded by it, and a deadline passed while waiting for a pooled connection is answered `lookup-timeout` though the same search may then answer.

The lookup deadline is a timer in the server process: if the process dies, its statement runs on, and PostgreSQL notices the gone client only when it sends, unless `client_connection_check_interval` is set.
PostgreSQL lookups run on a client of their own, so each allowlisted PostgreSQL database may use up to twice the connections it did.

The PostgreSQL adapter cancels a lookup through three private properties of postgres.js 3.4.9 (`state`, `describeFirst`, `canceller`), so a driver upgrade that changes them fails its suite and changes 0061.

A PostgreSQL lookup abandoned before it was sent is still sent and then stopped, and one aborted before PostgreSQL described it may be sent a second cancel request, which can stop the next lookup on that backend.
A PostgreSQL lookup stopped by another lookup's late cancel, or by a role-level `statement_timeout`, runs a second time; one stopped twice is answered `unavailable`.
postgres.js keeps the FATAL of a PostgreSQL backend an operator terminates and gives it, unsent, to the first statement on the next connection it opens, a record's statement included.

Behind a proxy, an abandoned search stops in the database only if the proxy closes its upstream connection when its client goes; nothing tests the composed stack's nginx or the Cloudflare edge for it.
A lookup refused for its deadline reaches the person as the renderer's "The options could not be loaded. Type to try again.", and typing more does not make a contains search cheaper.
A page of records searches as a lookup does and has neither cancellation nor a deadline.
On SQL Server, mssql's default request timeout of 15 s still cuts any lookup deadline set above it, answered `unavailable`.
An abandoned lookup is answered 499 `abandoned`, a status no standard names, which appears only in the audit trail.
An imported version keeps its connection's and its form's names, so both deployments' allowlists give the database the same name, and renaming one is an allowlist edit and a restart.

A version file is refused by a deployment whose release generates another base or other bindings from the same snapshot and request, so both deployments run releases that generate alike, or the form is proposed again in the target.

An imported version serves, and drifts against, the snapshot the source deployment took, its account's name and its whole scope, until it is regenerated in the target, and a target account narrower than the source's is drift that refuses the import.
A version file holds the snapshot's metadata and the role names its policy grants, so where it is kept is the team's to secure.
Importing the same file again writes a new version, as a restore of the same version does.
Nothing proves where a version file came from: the import checks what it holds, and each deployment's trail says only who read it there and who imported it here.
Each import discovers the target database once, and a database that cannot be reached refuses it.
Under review an import is a draft, which discovers the target database at its submit and again at its approval, and a database that cannot be reached refuses either.

A change to the default lookup deadline alone does not mark the published performance figures stale: the file that holds it is left out of the measured product, because a measurement runs the server with the longest deadline a timer holds; the default is held instead to equal what the committed figures derive.

The release notes of 0.1.0 are a summary written by hand: why each change before it was made is in CHANGELOG.md under Development before 0.1.0, not on the release page, and nothing checks that the summary says what those entries say.
Publication is reviewed only when FORMANCY_DATA_PUBLISHER_ROLES is set, so a deployment that upgrades without setting it lets every administrator publish, import and restore alone, as before.
Nobody approves a draft they submitted, whatever roles they hold, so a deployment under review needs a publisher besides each draft's author.
A publisher restores any version alone, one published by a single administrator before review was turned on included.
No route shows a publisher a draft's drift before approval: what blocks refuses the approval, and what drift only asks to review is in the approval's answer, after the version is written.
A publisher approves a draft with the reassigned keys its author confirmed, not with a confirmation of their own.
Publisher roles, like administrator roles, are read only from the token's roles claim, so an identity provider that puts roles elsewhere maps them into it.

Under review every submit and every approval discovers the database, so one that cannot be reached refuses both, and a version is written only while drift against the database blocks nothing, which a direct publish without review does not ask.

A draft reads published when the version after its base holds the same bundle, so two drafts of one bundle on one base both read published once either is approved, and so does a rejected draft of that bundle.
A draft whose base another version replaced, by another approval or a restore, is stale and can be neither approved nor rejected; it is submitted again over the newest version.

An approval and a rejection of the same draft at the same moment can both succeed, because the two writes go to two stores that share no compare-and-swap: the version is written, the rejection answers 201, and the draft then reads published.
Who approved a version is recorded only as the actor of the audit trail's draft-approve event; the version file is the bundle alone.
A pending draft notifies nobody: it waits until a publisher opens the queue.

Nothing deletes a draft: rejected, published and stale drafts stay on the volume, and the queue and every draft route read all of a form's entries, the queue every form's, on every request, a cost not measured.
A form one of whose draft entries no longer parses or validates on the volume serves none of its drafts and takes no new one until the file is put right, and the queue names it as unreadable.
Turning review off leaves the drafts on the volume, where no route reads or publishes them until it is turned on again.
The composed stack and the getting-started guide run without review, which the data server's README describes and its suites hold, and no gate runs it in the composed stack.

A ConfigurationStore an embedder implements must now provide drafts(), and code that builds an AdminAuditEvent or narrows its operation exhaustively meets the event's draft field and the administration and draft operations, review or not.
The studio's Review step shows a draft's form on paper, its submitter, base, confirmed keys and policy, and not what it changes from the version it replaces.
Every lookup that can be searched is a typeahead, a short list included; an administrator cannot choose a plain list for one.
A lookup that shows no text or whole-number column is a plain select of its first page, and a row past it cannot be chosen.
A lookup cannot show a binary, rowversion or unsupported column, which no label can spell: the generator refuses it, and the studio offers such a column disabled.

When a plain select's search fails, the database out of reach for one, it says the renderer's own sentence that its options could not be loaded and are asked for again each time the person moves to the field, and it asks again only then: a person who stays on the select sees the failure until they leave it and come back.

A form published at 0.1.0 names no typeahead, so every host, the reference host page now included, draws its lookups as plain selects of their first page until it is regenerated and published again; restoring such a version brings them back.
A version file exported from 0.1.0 is refused by this release's import, so the source deployment upgrades and regenerates first, or the form is proposed again in the target.

A version published before this release whose lookup shows a binary, rowversion or unsupported column is still served, and its list still cannot be built; regenerating it leaves that lookup out, and this release's import refuses its version file.
The regeneration report does not say that a republish changes a lookup's control.

Only the adapter suites and data-fixtures run on every image of each engine's matrix: the server, client, host, studio and performance suites, the browser gates and the composed stack run each engine's default image alone, so what the routes, the client and the pages do on another version is not tested.
PostgreSQL 14 and older, and SQL Server 2017 and older, are not images of the matrix, and a release is not tested on them.
What the versions of one engine disagree on is named only where a test has met it: a difference no suite reaches is in no table, and the release report prints none of them.

On PostgreSQL 18 a cascaded table's AFTER DELETE trigger runs with its owner's grants, so a delete that 15 to 17 refuse, `permission-denied`, because the trigger writes where the deleting account may not, is done.

Nothing refuses a server this release was not tested on: a form is generated, published and served on one as on a server it was tested on, and the runtime plane never discovers again, so a server upgraded in place is seen only by the next discovery, and a person filling a form is never told.
A managed PostgreSQL, or any server whose `version()` begins "PostgreSQL ", reads as PostgreSQL of its major, and as tested, whatever else it changed.

A SQL Server database is called tested at any compatibility level from the lowest a matrix leg's fixture database answered upward, on any tested release, though each leg's fixture runs at its release's own default level.

SQL Server discovery refuses a server whose catalog has no `sys.edge_constraints`, every release before 2019, naming its release, so no form is generated from SQL Server 2017 or older; no such server answered a test here: the refusal's sentence and condition are held by a unit test, and that discovery throws it before reading the catalog is held by nothing.
A snapshot taken before 0068 records no server, so whether the release was tested on it cannot be said until it is discovered again.

Drift review lists a `server-untested` change, for review, on every review of every form whose current snapshot names a server this release was not tested on, an unchanged catalog included, for as long as that server and this release stay as they are; of a snapshot that records no server it says nothing.

An administrator is told that this release was not tested on a server by the connection test, the studio and drift review; a server it was not tested on is answered, discovered, published and imported as any other.
A posted bundle's `server` is the client's: outside the fingerprint, it is checked for its shape alone, and only a fresh discovery speaks for the server.

An embedder's own `DatabaseAdapter` must report `product` and `major`, and for SQL Server `compatibility`, from `ping`, since `ServerIdentity` now extends `ServerFacts`; and an exhaustive `switch` over `DriftKind` must handle its new `server-untested`.
The demo at formancy.ai/data/examples/ is the examples page as main holds it, deployed by Cloudflare on every push without waiting for that commit's CI, so it can show what no release has published.

What formancy.ai/data/examples/ serves was read by hand once, on 2026-10-16 -- the notices as UTF-8 text, a 404 under the path with the demo's headers, the redirect of the path without its slash with none -- and nothing in this repository reads it since: a header a later deploy, Cloudflare or a setting of the zone changes fails nothing, and a failed deploy leaves the last one serving with its log in Cloudflare's dashboard.

The demo's Content-Security-Policy allows scripts, styles and fetches from all of formancy.ai's origin, the report's Studio and whatever is routed there later included, not only the demo's path, because a policy held to the path could not be measured in a gate that serves the page from 127.0.0.1.

Cloudflare's bot detection puts an inline script into the demo's page as it is served, and the page's Content-Security-Policy refuses it, as read on 2026-10-16: the browser's console shows that refusal on every load, Cloudflare gets no bot signal from the demo, and the browser gate, which serves the page itself, never sees it; letting it run would take 'unsafe-inline' or a nonce made per request by code the Worker does not have, and turning detection off would change formancy.ai's whole zone.
The demo is a page on formancy.ai's hostname without the site's shell: no site bar, no site footer and no link back to formancy.ai.
The demo Worker's build settings are in Cloudflare's dashboard, where nothing here reads them; a test holds only what .github/REPO-METADATA.md records of them.
Workers Builds reads this repository through the Cloudflare Workers and Pages GitHub app, whose access is a setting of the rightsholder's GitHub account that nothing here reads.
The demo Worker's compatibility date stays until someone reads what moving it changes, and which of Cloudflare's changes tied to that date reach a Worker with no code was not read.

The demo's THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt names the exact version of every package the examples page bundles, to anyone, and the repository's own LICENSE.md and NOTICE are reached through the page's link to the repository, not served beside it.
The data: images the demo's policy allows are drawn only by Safari on a touch device, which no browser gate runs, so that allowance is held by deriving it from the stylesheets, not by a browser.

The examples gate audits with axe's preload off, which was measured to change no rule's outcome on the page on 2026-10-16, and would audit less a page that gained media or a cross-origin stylesheet a rule reads.
The examples gate fails on any console error in any browser, so a browser release that logs a new one fails it until someone reads why.

The examples gate's check of what the browser refused holds the page's code and not axe's: what Playwright evaluates, axe included, was measured to run outside the page's Content-Security-Policy in Chromium and Firefox.

The live demo at formancy.ai/data/demo/ needs the rightsholder's Cloudflare account on the Workers Paid plan, $5 a month, and is billed while anybody uses it: at the prices read on 2026-10-16 a visit of ten minutes' use costs about $0.0037 once the plan's included amounts, about 67 such visits a month, are spent, and ten servers running a whole 30-day month cost at most $201.66 with every CPU busy, beside the Worker's requests and the Durable Objects' requests, storage writes and alarms -- a key and an alarm for every start that answers, the alarm run a day later -- which were not computed.

Anybody can start a live demo server and one visitor can take every one of the ten places, after which every other sign-in is refused, with the one sentence every failed start gets, until a server stops; a rate limiting rule of the zone on the sign-in is the operator's to add, and nothing here sets or reads it.

Everything a visitor changes in the live demo is gone when their server stops, 10 minutes after its Durable Object goes inactive, which Cloudflare documents as 10 s to 140 s after their last request and nobody has measured, and on every deploy whose image changed, which restarts every running demo server at once.
The live demo runs PostgreSQL alone: nothing of SQL Server is on it.

A live demo visitor's first sign-in waits for their own server to start, 5.7 to 11.7 s through the Worker at basic's CPU and memory share on a workstation over four runs on 2026-10-17, and is refused past 60 s (0087), which a start took there on a busy Docker engine; on Cloudflare neither a start nor a request's way through the Worker and the Durable Object has been measured.
