Cloudflare runs the live demo's Worker, a Durable Object per visitor and their containers on formancy.ai's zone, decrypts every request at its edge, and holds whatever a visitor types, personal data included, in their container until it stops.

The live demo's one cookie, `__Secure-formancy-data-demo`, is the only credential of a visitor's server: whoever holds it while that browser keeps it can sign in to that server and read and change what the visitor changed.

A live demo token lasts an hour and the page does not renew it: a visit that goes on longer is refused, 401, by a server that still runs, until the visitor signs out and signs in again, which reaches the same server.

The live demo's Worker checks only the shape of the name in its cookie, so a script can address, and on Cloudflare create, Durable Objects by names of its own choosing, each a billed Durable Object request, and start a container in one by signing in; that reaches no other visitor's server, whose name is 128 random bits.
With observability off, Cloudflare keeps no log of the live demo's Worker or containers, so a failed start is diagnosed by reproducing it, with the line it writes to the Worker's live log (0086).
The live demo's Content-Security-Policy allows inline styles, for the style elements AG Grid injects, where the examples page's allows none.

Each deploy whose live demo image changed pushes another image of about 198 MB compressed, as `gzip -1` of `docker save` measured it on 2026-10-16, into the account's 50 GB, and old ones are deleted by hand.
The live demo's server stops a lookup after 3,568 ms, four times the product's default, because its container has a quarter of a CPU.

The live demo is main's server, image and page, which Workers Builds builds whole and deploys on every push without waiting for CI, beside the examples page's build and against the same build minutes, and whether its build fits Workers Builds' 20-minute limit is first read in the first build's log.

The live demo's Durable Object code is held by review: its gate runs the Worker's module over a stand-in for Cloudflare's runtime whose containers are `docker run`s under CPU and memory quotas, which takes no network away, stops nothing when idle and caps nothing, and what Cloudflare answers at the cap and how long a server outlives its visitor are read once, by hand, after the first deploy.

The live demo's page is measured in Chromium alone, by its gate, and the ordinary host build, which leaves out the demo's wiring and `src/demo.ts`, carries the persona sign-in it never draws, as its chunks were read on 2026-10-17, which nothing checks.
The live demo's PostgreSQL is not among the servers the release report says the run was tested on.

`FORMANCY_DATA_TRUSTED_PROXIES` believes every address in its list about the clients behind it: a list too wide lets a client that connects from inside it choose its own rate-limit bucket and the address the log names, and one too narrow counts everybody behind the proxy it leaves out as one client, which nothing reports.
The trusted proxies are read at start, so changing them is a restart; they are not read again on SIGHUP.

A proxy that passes a client's `X-Forwarded-For` on without appending the address it saw is never safe to name: an address the client wrote is then believed, and nothing tells such a proxy from one that appends.

Only `X-Forwarded-For` is read for a client's address, as Fastify reads it, not RFC 7239's `Forwarded`, `X-Real-IP` or `CF-Connecting-IP`, and a forwarded value that is not an IP address -- an address with its port among them -- is counted and logged as the proxy's.
A client is its address: people behind one NAT or one proxy of their own share a rate-limit bucket, and an IPv6 client is counted by its /64.
With a proxy trusted, the server's log names each client's address where it named the proxy's -- behind the tunnel, each visitor's -- which is personal data, kept as long as the log is.

Behind the tunnel the server believes the visitor's address Cloudflare's edge puts in `X-Forwarded-For`, as Cloudflare documents it and not measured here, and a private network route to the tunnel would let an enrolled device name an address of its own choice there.

Two stacks from `compose.yaml` do not run at once on one machine, the getting-started gate's included, and on a machine where another network holds 172.16.238.0/24 or 172.16.239.0/24 the stack does not start until that network is removed or five values in two files are changed together.
From a trusted proxy, Fastify's `request.host` and `request.protocol` follow `X-Forwarded-Host` and `X-Forwarded-Proto`, which nginx passes on from any client; nothing in the server reads either.

The studio, the host page and the examples page bundle the Archivo, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono fonts under the SIL Open Font License 1.1, not this repository's licence, and the notices beside each page carry that licence's text.
The pages' fonts are the Fontsource release the workspace catalog pins, so a fix Google ships to a face reaches them only when this repository moves the pins, and nothing says one is due.
Each app's build carries 59 font files, 757,316 bytes, and the web image two such sets, most of them subsets and WOFF fallbacks no visitor's browser fetches (measured with Vite 8.3.3 on 2026-10-16).
On a machine with a font installed under the name Archivo, the studio, the host page and the examples page draw their headings in that font rather than the face they carry.

That no page asks another host for anything is held by the browser gates for the states they reach and by a static read of each index.html and built stylesheet, not of the JavaScript, where the host page's bundle holds AG Grid's loader of Google's fonts, unused: a request only an interaction the gates do not perform makes, or a connection with no request, is seen by nothing.

Neither Azure SQL Database nor Azure SQL Managed Instance answered any test: SQL Server is tested in containers only, so discovery, the record operations, `rowversion`, triggers, row-level security and a lookup's cancellation are proved on neither.

Azure SQL Database and Azure SQL Managed Instance are called not tested at the major of every SQL Server release this release can name and every major either engine was tested at, at none, and at every compatibility level from 100 to 180, so an estate on either is told so by every connection test and, as `server-untested`, on every drift review of every form published from it.

What Azure SQL answers -- `EngineEdition` 5 for Azure SQL Database and 8 for Managed Instance, and Azure SQL Database's `ProductVersion` 12.0 -- is taken from Microsoft's documentation and not measured here, so a service that answered otherwise would be read wrongly and nothing here would know; what either answers for `ProductMajorVersion`, which Microsoft documents for SQL Server alone, is not documented at all.

Every boxed SQL Server -- `EngineEdition` 2, 3 or 4, on any host, Windows or Linux, in any edition, SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines among them -- is called tested when its release and its database's compatibility level are, though every test ran the Developer edition on Linux in a container.

Under Azure SQL's Redirect connection policy a client goes on from port 1433 to a port from 11000 to 11999, and a paused serverless database answers error 40613 while it resumes, both as Microsoft documents them; no test meets either, so what a connection test, a discovery or a record request answers then is not known.

The allowlist accepts an Entra managed identity or service principal for a SQL Server connection, and no test logs in with either: the tests show only that a SQL Server 2025 container started with a certificate refuses such a login over TDS 8.0, that nothing is retried as a SQL login and that no secret is written.

An Entra login goes over TDS 8.0 alone, TLS before the first TDS message, so a server that does not take it cannot be reached as an Entra principal: of the images measured on 2026-10-17, SQL Server 2019 and 2022 on Linux reset the connection, and 2025 did too without a certificate configured.
An Entra token is asked for Azure SQL's resource in the public cloud alone, so Azure Government's and Azure China's are refused, and a tenant is named by its id, never by its domain name.
An Entra connection refuses TLS turned off and a trusted server certificate, so a server whose certificate is self-signed, or re-signed by a proxy, cannot be reached as an Entra principal.

An allowlist with a key this release does not read, at an entry, in `tls` or in `login`, or a `tls` setting that is not true or false, stops the server at start, naming the key: a file with a stray key that an earlier release started with no longer starts.

A managed identity entry stops the server at start while `AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE` is set, as AKS workload identity sets it, so such a pod logs in as a service principal or not at all; the check is the runnable server's, and an embedder's own composition root does not have it.

Only the first connection of an Entra pool says why its login failed: a login refused later, when the pool opens another connection, is `unavailable` on a record request, but discovery's log line then gives no reason.

A connection's Entra credential and the token it caches are kept while its secret is the same, so a change to the principal in Entra that the token carries, its groups among them, reaches a connection opened again after a failure only when that token is refreshed.
A service principal's secret file that cannot be read is named in the server's log line, as a password's file is; a resolved secret's path is written nowhere.

A managed identity off Azure failed to get a token in 0.00 to 0.02 s on a Windows 11 host and in 4.53 to 6.37 s in the server image's base under Docker Desktop, measured on 2026-10-17, inside mssql's 15 s connect timeout; a host that drops packets to the metadata address rather than refusing them was not measured, and could fail the login as a timeout naming the host instead.

@azure/identity and MSAL read the region, the proxy and the log level from the environment for any Entra login, and a managed identity its platform's endpoint, outside the reviewed allowlist; `AZURE_LOG_LEVEL` writes their lines to standard error, outside the server's log.
@azure/identity is a dependency of `@formancy/data-sqlserver` at exactly 4.13.3, so a fix to it reaches an installation only through a release of this module that moves the version.
An embedder's `ConnectionConfig.user` and `password` are optional beside `login`, and a `ConnectionFactory` of their own is given its secret as `string | undefined`.

The README's tested-on row calls the SQL login tested from a value typed in `SQLSERVER_LOGINS`: no server record says which login a test made, so the release report does not say that every SQL Server login of a run was a SQL login.
A section keeps at least one field, so a section's only field, often Record's `id`, cannot move out of it, and no section can be emptied or removed.
A field moved to another section lands last in it, and a person places it from there with Move up.

A 0.1.0 server refuses to read or import a version holding a move between sections, naming `/fields/N/section`, as measured on 2026-10-16, so a deployment rolled back to 0.1.0 stops serving such a newest version until an earlier one is restored there; versions without a move move between them as before.

A regeneration drops a move into a section it no longer has or cannot tell apart, and every move out of a section the carried moves would leave with no field, not the fewest, reporting each as `move-dropped`; the person moves the field again.
The studio's Move to buttons name a section by its current label, so two sections a person labelled alike read alike.
A field's help text is not offered: `@formancy/spec` 0.5.0 has no property to hold it.

0076.none: A rule for this repository's documentation: the architecture sections and the guard that holds them are read by contributors, reviewers and evaluators, and nobody who installs, integrates or operates the module meets their costs.

limitations.says: On PostgreSQL 18 a column with a `NOT NULL` added `NOT VALID` is generated optional until `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` runs, so a create or an update that leaves it empty is refused by the database, `not-null-violation`, where the form would have said a value is required, and a key over it lists no page and it is not offered as a version column.

On PostgreSQL 18 create is offered over a table with a `NOT NULL` added `NOT VALID` over a column no field writes on create -- of a type no codec reads, unreadable or not insertable -- and with no default, and the database refuses every create, `not-null-violation`, unless a trigger fills the column, where the column read `NOT NULL` kept create from being offered; the same holds on every version for the rule spelled as a check, which the generator does not read.

Validating a `NOT NULL` added `NOT VALID` on PostgreSQL 18 tightens its column, which drift review reports and which blocks the writes of a form that writes it, and the create of a form no field of which writes it on create, until the form is reviewed.

A form published on PostgreSQL 18 before 0077 over a column with a `NOT NULL` added `NOT VALID` reads that column as loosened and a check as new: keyed by a unique key over the column, it lists no page until the constraint is validated, though a record is still read by its token; with the column as its version column, it has update and delete blocked, and a review cannot confirm the column again until the constraint is validated; and where its control cannot hold NULL -- a boolean shown as a checkbox -- its writes of the column are blocked until it is reviewed.

The expression of a `NOT NULL` added `NOT VALID` is spelled by the PostgreSQL adapter as `pg_get_expr` spells the same check on 18, and a later version that deparsed it otherwise would differ from the hand-written check unseen until a test ran on it.

The PostgreSQL adapter's catalog reads -- discovery's, and the server's version read -- still take postgres.js 3.4.9's array of rows, so one that failed part-way would leave the next catalog read on its connection behind empty slots, and no test shows what discovery then does.

An integrator's own statements on a client it also hands the PostgreSQL adapter get their rows as postgres.js 3.4.9 gives them: after a statement on the same connection that ended part-way, behind one empty slot for each row it sent.

A file of records is refused past 16 MiB of UTF-8 (`422 export-too-large`) or 30 seconds (`503 export-timeout`): a memory budget and a proxy's default less a driver's, neither a measurement of what an export of a given size finishes in.
One file of records is made at a time per allowlisted connection in each server process; another meanwhile is refused `503 export-busy`, and each replica has a gate of its own.

An export refused at its deadline or left by its client keeps its connection's gate until the page it was running returns, so every other export through that connection is refused `503 export-busy` meanwhile: on SQL Server for at most mssql's 15 seconds, on PostgreSQL for as long as that statement runs, a lock wait included.

Each page of a file reads every row before its offset, about n²/100 rows for a file of n, and a sort no index serves reads every admitted row on every page; by how both engines run an offset, not measured.
A file of records is not the table at one moment: each page is its own statement, so a row deleted meanwhile before an offset is skipped unseen, and one inserted there refuses the file `409 moved`.

A text cell of a file that starts with `=`, `+`, `-`, `@`, TAB, CR or an apostrophe, and is not a number, carries one apostrophe more than the database holds, which a spreadsheet may show; one that starts with a space or a full-width `＝` carries none.
A file holds an instant to the second and a time to the minute, as a read does, and its header can repeat a label, which some importers refuse.
On SQL Server an unpaired surrogate or a NUL in any text a file would hold refuses the whole file `409 unencodable`, though the JSON list carries both.

A lookup whose key needs more characters as a token than a token holds refuses the whole file `409 unencodable`, though the grid shows the row, so one such row stops every file of the form that would hold it.

What a spreadsheet does with a file is not tried, so none of this is shown here: Excel is expected to show `9007199254740993` to 15 significant digits, which the file does not, not to tell `""` from NULL, and in a locale whose list separator is `;` to open the file as one column; a reader that does not expect a byte-order mark glues it to the first header.
No policy lets a person browse a form's records and not download them: whoever may list may download, and only a proxy can drop the route, for everybody.
A lookup filter the policy refuses a person refuses their file of records, where the grid shows that lookup's tokens.
On PostgreSQL nothing bounds a list statement, so an export page that runs past nginx's 60-second read timeout gets the person nginx's 504 while the server makes a file for nobody.
Every runtime audit event carries `rows`, `null` but for an export, which a deployment's own sink sees; an export's `ok` says the server sent the whole file, not that the browser kept it.
A form that binds a column with no text -- which only a format-1 bundle edited where it is stored can -- answers its file 500, and no file.
Leaving a form, signing out or opening another parent while Download CSV makes a file drops the file, and the page says nothing; pressing again makes it.

Download CSV says the page handed the file to the browser, not that the browser saved it: a browser that asks where to save, a person who cancels, or a download the browser blocks is heard by nothing.
Download CSV says the name of the file and not how many records it holds.
The host page holds the whole file in memory before the browser saves it, up to the server's `EXPORT_MAX_BYTES`.

The host page saves a file through an object URL and a clicked anchor, which the browser gate measures in Playwright's Chromium, Firefox and Linux WebKit; Safari and the browsers on a phone are not tried.

A SQL Server that cannot encrypt, answering NOT_SUP to a SQL login that asks for TLS, is refused on every connection, where 0.1.0 logged in to it unencrypted; reaching it takes `tls.enabled: false`, which sends the login unencrypted by that choice.
A SQL login with `tls.enabled: false`, the composed stack's among them, still sends its login unencrypted to whoever answers, by the operator's choice: only a connection that asks for TLS is guarded.

With `tls.trustServerCertificate` true, whoever answers in the server's place can still complete TLS with a certificate of its own and read a SQL login: the guard checks that TLS starts, not with whom.

A SQL login with TLS on connects through the adapter's own copy of tedious's `connectInSequence`, so a later fix tedious makes to how it connects does not reach those connections until it is copied, and nothing says one was made.

Every byte a SQL Server sends on a connection with TLS on passes through one more stream, the guard's, for the life of the connection, each chunk queued and emitted once more and only the reads carrying the server's first message copied; a measurement on a shared machine on 2026-10-17 could not tell what that costs from the spread between its own rounds, and none was made on a quiet one.

Only a pool's first connect says the refusal in the adapter's sentence alone: a connection the pool opens later and the guard refuses is `unavailable` on a record request, and discovery's log line says tedious's "Connection lost - " before the sentence, by the code and not tried.

The guard is written against what tedious 20.3.3 uses of its socket and how it reads the PRELOGIN answer: a release that changes either is caught as far as the suites through the guard reach, and nothing shows tedious refusing the downgrade itself, since the guard refuses first.

0082.none: Test support for this repository's suites: data-fixtures is never published, and nobody who installs, integrates or operates the module starts its containers or reads how one that failed to start is reported.

limitations.says: A script injected into the composed stack's studio or host page -- by a browser extension that writes a script element, a proxy in front that adds an inline one, or a page that wraps the host page -- does not run under the page's Content-Security-Policy, and only the browser's console says so.

The host page's policy allows inline styles, for the style elements AG Grid creates, where the studio's allows none: a style injected into the host page can restyle it, though it can load nothing from another host.
A host page served on an origin of its own, as 0060 allows, needs a policy whose connect-src names the server's origin; the composed stack's refuses that call, and no gate runs it.

A deployment's own proxy sends the pages their policies only if it copies the header from deploy/web/nginx.conf, and nothing here reads what a deployment sends; 'self' there is its whole origin, so other files it serves on that origin are scripts the pages may load.

WebKit ran the studio's and the host page's gates under their policies once off CI, in Playwright's own Linux image on 2026-10-17, before CI's WebKit leg; and what the composed stack's nginx sends is read by the getting-started gate in CI, which was not run where the change was made.

The studio's and the host page's gates read what each document was refused after its last measured state, just before the canary, and the canary fails on anything left before it; a refusal whose report is still on its way when that last read is made -- the canary's own took 0.5 to 7.1 ms in Chromium -- is heard by nothing.

A release may be published with docs/performance.md measured on an earlier product: nothing refuses it, and only the page's When and on what -- the commit and the drivers it measured -- and the version's changelog section, which review alone holds, say so.

The default lookup deadline is derived from the committed figures (0063), so in a release whose figures are an earlier product's it is what those figures derived, not what this release's lookups were measured taking.
A lookup says that more rows match than its page shows, never how many.

A typeahead says that more rows match only while its list is open, and every reference theme of formancy 0.6.0 and 0.7.0 draws the open list over that sentence, so a sighted person does not read it; a screen reader hears it from the field’s status line, and a plain select’s sentence is seen.
Rows whose labels agree beyond one page are reached by typing only through a display column that tells them apart.
A row whose key does not fit a token is said to the person, with a count only when no more rows match, and never offered.

`@formancy/data-client` states the lookup page its own release’s server answers, so a host whose client and server are of releases with different page sizes would have its searches refused or cut short; no release has changed the page size.
The examples page’s source says that more rows match, as a database’s does, though it holds every row and could count them.
A failed start of the live demo is said only in the Worker's live log, to whoever runs wrangler tail while it happens; nothing keeps it, and the container's own output is still nobody's.
Whoever can tail the live demo's Worker reads Cloudflare's error for a failed start as Cloudflare wrote it, with the start's key cut out of it.
A live demo sign-in whose start fails is answered after up to 60 s, and the page still says a first start takes a few seconds.
A running live demo visitor's Durable Object is held from eviction while its container runs, up to 15 minutes, by the monitor() it waits on, and Cloudflare bills that as Durable Object duration.
A live demo start Cloudflare has no instance for is told by an undocumented sentence of Cloudflare's; reworded, such a start is said as a failed container and not started again.

0088.none: A fix of the demo image's start and of the gate's fidelity to Cloudflare: nothing a visitor or an operator meets. What else Cloudflare's VM starts differently from Docker is 0070's cost that the Durable Object's code and the image on Cloudflare are read after a deploy.

0089.none: A grant of the live demo's own account: nothing a user, integrator or operator of a release meets. The generator is unchanged, so a deployment's own column with a default is still offered wherever its account may INSERT it, as 0027 says.

limitations.says: Drill down's levels are in the page's memory only: a reload, or a link sent to someone, opens the form's records, and the path down has to be walked again.
One Back after a record is deleted at a Drill down level can show nothing new: the entry it lands on is the level the delete replaced.
A child row open on a section's rail in another layout and the same row opened a level down in Drill down are two forms with their own unsaved changes, and the unsaved-changes notice names both.
Drill down's trail names a record by the first required plain text field of its form, which can be a field a person would not have chosen, and by its token when no field qualifies.
On a phone the four layouts of the Layout group take two rows.
A product that verifies host tokens with `@formancy/data-identity` accepts what the data server accepts only while both install the same release of it; nothing checks that they do.

The first release that publishes `@formancy/data-identity` creates its name on npm, which a Granular Access token limited to the packages it names may not do, and the `npm-token` job does not check for that.

A release's SBOM lists the versions a clean npm install of its packages resolved on the day it was made; a runtime dependency may be newer than the version the suites ran, which the release body names as run by no suite.
A release's SBOM leaves out packages of TypeScript declarations alone, such as `@types/mssql`, which a consumer's type checker reads and no code of which runs.
A release's SBOM leaves out the peers its packages name, which the host installs.
A form published before 0093 over a column named `__proto__` is refused when it is read, and leaves the menu, until it is published again under the key `__proto___`.
The field over a column named `__proto__` is keyed `__proto___`, so a host's own code, draft or rule that named the key `__proto__` names nothing.

A form published before 0095 keeps a nullable yes/no column's radio group until it is published again: its answer cannot be taken back to no answer, and a rule that disables it does not stop a choice, which the server then refuses for a field the person may not write.
A nullable yes/no field is a select, which shows the answer given and opens for the others, where a radio group showed both.
A nullable yes/no field is drawn only in the examples' jsdom tests: no table of the shared model has a nullable boolean column, so the host's suites and the browser gates never draw one.

The examples page, the studio and the host page draw with formancy's admin palette at the `@formancy/themes` release this repository pins, so a palette change upstream reaches them only with the version bump that brings it.
The studio's page carries the `--wb-*` variables formancy's `room.css` sets for the builder's panes, which it does not load, so they recolour nothing.

A changed value in a field the person may not write, sent with a version the record no longer holds, is answered 409 stale rather than 403 over-posting, so such tampering is told only that its version is old; nothing is written.

A row a Drill down level holds, deleted while the person goes down into it and types there, takes that typing with it once the delete is done, without a word; its confirmation named only what the levels held when it was asked or Delete it was pressed.

In a layout that moves between none of them, Back takes one press for each Separate views view or Drill down level the open form's history holds, shows nothing new on each, and writes the layout shown over those entries, so Forward no longer brings their views or levels back.

A holder of a role FORMANCY_DATA_BROWSE_ROLES names reads every row of every table and view in the approved schemas that the connection's account can read, with no form, policy, row filter or field rule between; give the role to few people, or browse through a connection whose account may read less.
Every page a browse shows discovers the connection's whole scope again before its statement, with nothing cached between pages, so a catalog with many objects makes every page slower; not measured.
A view, or a table with no key the account may read, is browsed in the order of every column shown, and rows equal in all of them may trade places between pages.

A browse shows no binary, rowversion or unsupported column and none the account may not select, naming each; it has no row count, no filter beyond the search, no export and no editing, and the studio sorts by one column at a time.
The audit trail names the connection and the object a browse read, never its search, its sort, a row or how many rows.
A trusted-proxy list that covers all but part of a family's addresses, such as half of IPv4 and a quarter more, still starts: only a list that trusts every IPv4 or every IPv6 peer is refused.

A browsed row is followed only through a foreign key whose columns are all of a key kind -- text, integer, decimal, uuid or date -- so a key over a timestamp, a boolean or binary is named in the Browse step and not followed.

A foreign key through a column the connection's account may not read at either end, one to or from a table outside the approved schemas, and one onto a table the account cannot see are each named in the Browse step and not followed.
A relationship the catalog does not declare as a foreign key, such as a column naming another table's row by convention or anything a view joins, is not offered to follow.
A row whose foreign key holds a NULL in any column follows nothing through it, since it refers to no row on either engine, even where its other columns would find rows.

A follow compares the row's values with each engine's own equality, as the foreign key does, so under a case- or accent-insensitive collation it finds the rows the key would match and not only those spelled the same.
A foreign key the database does not enforce, or has not validated, is offered to follow as any other, and a follow through it finds what the row's values find, which may be nothing.

Where a table the connection's account cannot see may refer to the browsed object, or its snapshot does not record what refers to each table, the Browse step says that the keys referring to it may not all be offered.

The studio offers the follows its own discovery holds, so a column dropped or made unreadable since is refused by the server as not-comparable when followed, a key dropped since still narrows by its columns, and a key added since is not offered until the studio discovers again.
Following what refers to a row narrows the referring table by the key's columns, which neither engine indexes on its own, so it may read the whole table where nobody made such an index; not measured.
The trail of follows lives in the page, so a reload loses it along with the sign-in.

The values a follow narrows by travel in the browse request's body and stand on the page, while the audit trail names only the connection and the object, never a value, so it cannot tell which row was followed.
A host token with a space, a newline or padding added on its way to the server, or written in base64 rather than base64url, is refused as malformed, though jose would have read some of those.
The composed stack does not run the server on a read-only root, though the image starts on one; an operator who wants it adds read_only and keeps the store's volume.

A filter's conditions are joined by AND: there is no OR, no not-equal, no starts-with and no range over text, and a field takes one condition, so a range is the way to say two things about one column.

A float, a time, binary, a rowversion and an unsupported column can be filtered only by whether they are empty, and only where they hold NULLs; a lookup field and a field the person may not read cannot be filtered at all.

Equality on text is exact on both engines, so typing muster ag does not find Muster AG even under a case-insensitive collation; contains folds case on both engines, and accents too on SQL Server where the column's collation does, never on PostgreSQL.
On PostgreSQL an unconstrained numeric keeps the scale each value was given, so an equality with 12.5 does not find a stored 12.50; a range compares them as numbers.

A timestamp offers no equality, only a range of whole days, and an instant's days are UTC's, as the page shows them, so a person thinking of their own day in another zone gets a range shifted by their offset.
A timestamp range to 9999-12-31 has no upper end, so on PostgreSQL it also holds a timestamp after the year 9999, which SQL Server cannot store.
A decimal with more fraction digits than its column holds, or a number outside its column's range or precision, is refused as not-filterable rather than rounded.

No plan of any filter is measured on either engine: contains reads every row the other conditions leave, and on SQL Server a datetime or smalldatetime column is converted to datetime2 to meet a day's bound, which may keep an index on it from being sought.
A condition the server refused stays in the host's list of conditions, and so in its grid's request and its file's, until the person replaces or removes it.

A person's own filter conditions are kept in no address and saved nowhere: a reload, another form, another parent for a child section and the studio's Show rows each start without them, though the host brings back a view the browser kept (0106).
@formancy/data-client refuses a form whose list says nothing of filters as unexpected, so a host upgrades its server before its client.
A list view is only what a person could have built: conditions joined by AND and an order, with no value relative to the day or to the person, so overdue or assigned to me cannot be a view.
A view's name is text in one language, not a translatable message.

Views are the same for everyone who may read their fields: none can be kept to a role, a person cannot save a view of their own, and only the viewer's browser remembers a picked one across a reload (0106).
A person who may not read a field a view names is not offered that view at all, not even without that condition, and a default view they are not offered leaves their grid opening on every record.
A view on a field nobody may read is stored and offered to nobody, and the studio says nothing of which roles will be offered which view.

Saving, removing and moving a view are not on the Presentation step's Undo and Redo, a view being defined and not saved is lost when the step is left, and a refusal is said with data-core's path counted from 0 and the field's key.
A stored view this release would not run, such as one a later release's tighter rule refuses, is not offered, and nothing says so to the person or in the log until a publish refuses it.
A regeneration or Generate again drops a view whose column is gone or no longer offers what it asks, rather than carrying it without that condition, and it has to be made again.
@formancy/data-client refuses a form whose list says nothing of views as unexpected, so a host upgrades its server before its client.
A grid's columns, sort and view are kept by the viewer's browser, not by the person: they follow nobody to another device, and everybody signed in on one browser profile shares them.
A person's own filter conditions are never kept, so a reload brings back their sort without them; a view is kept by its name, so a renamed one gives way to the default view.
Every child section of one form under one field shares one arrangement of columns, under every parent and at every level of Drill down.
A column's width is still its content's, and nothing is moved or resized by hand; search and page are not kept.
A hidden column is still read, its lookups resolved, and Download CSV holds every readable field whatever the grid hides.
A kept sort term no longer sortable is dropped and the rest kept, a kept view no longer offered gives the default view, both without a word, and a browser that keeps nothing says nothing of it.
Duplicate record copies a record alone, never its child rows, and a child row or a level of Drill down below the record offers none.
A copy leaves out every column of a primary or unique key, a part a person would keep included -- an order line's order beside its number -- which is chosen again.

A copy holds what a read returns: an instant to the second and a time to the minute are stored as shown, and a value no write accepts -- PostgreSQL's infinity, a 24:00 time -- has its create refused on that field until the person changes it.
@formancy/data-client refuses a form that offers create without saying what a copy carries as unexpected, so a host upgrades its server before its client.

A page continues after the row the page before ended with, wherever that row is now: edited between two pages in a column the list is sorted by, it moves the next page with it, and rows are skipped or shown again; a file refuses a record shown twice, never one skipped.
When the row the next page comes after has been deleted meanwhile, or is no longer one the person may read, the grid starts again at its first page, and a file of records is refused as moved.
Pages are walked, never jumped to: there is no page number, no total and no last page, and an order no index serves still reads and sorts every row the list admits for every page.
Browse still pages by offset, so a row inserted or deleted before a page between two pages shows a row twice or skips one.
The server refuses an older client's offset as malformed, and @formancy/data-client refuses an older server's page, which has no cursor, as unexpected, so a host and its server are upgraded together.
A record and its section are two forms with two saves, never one transaction, and the section is shown by the record as stored: a kind changed and not yet saved shows the section as it was.
A record whose kind changes away hides its section and keeps the section's row in the database, and a section offers no Delete; the section's own form, opened on its own, deletes it.
A section is shown by one column holding one value, or always; one whose column the parent's form does not show the person is shown always.
Drift review does not name a section's condition column: dropped or retyped, the section is shown always, and regenerating its form is refused until the condition is chosen again.
@formancy/data-client refuses a menu without its children's one and when as unexpected, so a host and its server are upgraded together.
A tree of records has no search, filter, sort or columns: each level is in key order and a record is its name, and the panel opens as a grid every time.
A record whose parent the person may not read, or that is gone, or that is in a cycle with no root, is in no level of the tree; the grid lists it.
A record of a composite self-reference is a root only with every column of its field NULL; one with some of them NULL is in no level of the tree.
Whether a record has records below it is known only once it is expanded, one list request per level, and the browser gates do not measure the tree.

The drift check needs the server running against the migrated database with its administrator's plane on, an administrator token, and the ids of the forms to check; it checks each form's published version, never a draft.
The drift check is a command in the server image, or in an installed @formancy/data-server, and prints lines for a log; a program reads the drift route's JSON instead.
A policy holds one field of a form to its moves, each a pair of values for named roles: no condition on another field, on time or on the person, and no move from any state.
A form offers every value its state field accepts; a move the person may not make is refused after Save with the policy's sentence, not withheld from the field's choices.
A create that leaves the state field to the column's default is not checked against the moves, and a write that reaches the table other than through the runtime plane is not checked at all.
An update whose record was read at a newer version than it names is answered stale, even where its move would be allowed from where the record is now.
The audit trail says that a create or an update moved the state field, never from where or to where; a deployment that needs the history keeps it in the database.
Moves are not a process engine: no task, assignment, deadline or notification follows a move.
A server older than this release refuses a policy that names moves, so a version holding them is not imported into an older deployment.

0114.none: How this repository's TypeScript and JavaScript are linted, formatted and merged across the format, which a contributor meets in every pull request -- a finding to fix, a file to format, a branch begun before the format merged through scripts/prettier-merge.mjs, a commit blame skips; the gate runs in CI, and the tools are root devDependencies no package declares. What reaches a user or an integrator is the CHANGELOG's -- the defects the linter found, fixed, and fieldHeading, which data-core now exports and data-client re-exports -- and none of it is a cost.
